headline: Middle East tensions spike as Houthis strike Riyadh and the US warns of rapid escalation — oil drops sharply despite the conflict heat, while your ASX ETFs finish the week on a solid note.

movers.name: Take-Two Interactive
movers.note: Take-Two slipped 2.45% in last night's session with no major company-specific news to explain the move — likely some broader risk-off selling. The long-term GTA VI release story remains intact. This is still a stock you hold for the game launch, not the day-to-day noise.

movers.name: Vanguard FTSE Emerging Markets ETF
movers.note: VGE had a solid session today, up 1.25%, likely catching a tailwind from a slightly firmer AUD and some positive momentum in emerging market assets. Nothing structural — just a good day for the fund.

movers.name: Global X Artificial Intelligence ETF
movers.note: GXAI closed up 1.15% today on the ASX, a decent bounce. AI sentiment continues to be broadly supportive, though the fund is still down about 11.7% from your purchase price. Long-term AI growth story remains the reason to hold.

movers.name: Pilbara Minerals
movers.note: PLS dipped another 1.18% today, continuing its weak run. Lithium prices remain soft globally and there's no near-term catalyst to reverse that. This is the portfolio's biggest loss (down 38%) but the long-term lithium demand story — driven by EVs and batteries — is a years-long thesis, not a quarters one.

movers.name: Vanguard Diversified High Growth ETF
movers.note: VDHG ticked up 0.53% today, a steady session. This diversified fund smooths out the rough edges of individual stock moves — exactly what it's designed to do.

movers.name: Vanguard US Total Market Shares ETF
movers.note: VTS gained 0.53% in today's ASX session, reflecting last night's positive US market close. The S&P 500 and NASDAQ both rose overnight, giving this fund a gentle lift.

movers.name: Microsoft
movers.note: Microsoft slipped 0.8% in last night's session — a mild pullback with no specific bad news attached. The stock is still up solidly from your entry price (about +11.4%). Nothing's changed with the long-term AI and cloud thesis.

movers.name: Alphabet Inc. (Google)
movers.note: GOOG nudged up 0.21% last night, a quiet but positive session. Google Cloud hit $20B in revenue this year and the stock remains about 12% above your cost basis. Steady as she goes.

watch_today.title: Oil down 5.7% despite Middle East escalation — watch this week
watch_today.detail: Crude oil (WTI) crashed from $101.91 to $96.08 a barrel last night — a 5.7% drop — even as Houthis attacked Riyadh and the US warned of rapid escalation. This is unusual: war-zone tension usually pushes oil UP. The drop suggests traders are worried more about demand weakening than supply disruption. Keep an eye on how this plays out — sustained high oil prices can feed into inflation and slow RBA rate cut hopes.

watch_today.title: TTWO — Hold through the dip, GTA VI thesis unchanged
watch_today.detail: Take-Two fell 2.45% last night with no company-specific bad news — just market noise. Your position is already down about 11.5% overall, but for a long-term investor the whole game here is the GTA VI release. That story hasn't changed. Sit tight.

watch_today.title: PLS.AX — Lithium still soft, but hold your nerve
watch_today.detail: Pilbara Minerals slipped another 1.18% today and is now down 38% from your cost price — the portfolio's biggest drag. Lithium prices remain depressed globally. However, the long-term case (EV batteries, energy storage) is a multi-year story. Selling now locks in the loss at the worst point of the cycle. Hold unless you need the cash.

watch_today.title: RBA may hike rates three more times — watch your mortgage and VGE
watch_today.detail: AFR reports traders are now pricing in three more RBA rate rises. That's bad news for anyone with a variable mortgage, and could put pressure on Australian growth assets. Your emerging markets ETF (VGE) had a good day today but could face headwinds if the Aussie dollar rises on rate expectations. Keep an eye on Tuesday's RBA commentary.

watch_today.title: GXAI.AX — AI lawsuit news is noise, hold the long-term bet
watch_today.detail: A major antitrust lawsuit has been filed against Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceX AI, alleging they illegally agreed to slow AI development. This is early-stage legal action and unlikely to derail the broader AI industry trend. Your GXAI ETF is still down about 11.7% but the long-term AI growth thesis remains intact. No action needed.

watch_today.title: MSFT — Mild dip, long-term story rock solid
watch_today.detail: Microsoft slipped 0.8% last night but remains up 11.4% from your entry price with no bad news attached. Azure cloud and Copilot AI integration continue to underpin the long-term case. Classic hold.

world.summary: The Middle East is the dominant global story today, with Houthi missile strikes on Saudi Arabia's capital and urgent US warnings of rapid escalation. World leaders are gathering at the UN against this backdrop. Meanwhile, California's governor is pushing back on federal election interference.

stories.title: Houthis launch missile strikes on Riyadh as US warns of rapid Mideast escalation
stories.why_it_matters: The Houthi rebel group (based in Yemen, backed by Iran) claimed responsibility for missile strikes on the Saudi capital Riyadh overnight, with flames and smoke visible near the city. The US responded by warning that the conflict 'has the potential to escalate rapidly' and President Trump cut short a stay at Camp David to deal with the crisis. This is a significant escalation of the broader Middle East war. For everyday Australians, a wider regional conflict involving Saudi Arabia risks disrupting global oil supply and could spike petrol prices — though ironically, oil actually fell sharply last night (see markets), suggesting traders are more focused on demand fears than supply shock for now.

stories.title: US warns of 'major escalation' in Iran war coming — what that means
stories.why_it_matters: US intelligence is signalling that a major escalation in the broader Iran-linked conflict is possible in coming days. The signs include an unusual pattern of Houthi attacks reaching deeper into Saudi territory, combined with diplomatic back-channels going quiet. For investors, a serious escalation could mean spiking oil and gold prices and a flight to safe-haven assets — which is worth watching given oil's strange drop today.

stories.title: World leaders return to UN General Assembly amid wars in Middle East and Ukraine
stories.why_it_matters: The UN General Assembly is meeting this week with global leaders gathering in New York against the backdrop of two major ongoing wars — the Middle East conflict and Russia's war in Ukraine. These annual meetings sometimes produce diplomatic breakthroughs or flashpoints. With both conflicts intensifying, expectations for progress are low, but the week's diplomacy could move markets if any surprise ceasefire or escalation occurs.

stories.title: California governor signs laws to block Trump's federal election interference
stories.why_it_matters: California Governor Gavin Newsom has signed a package of election security bills specifically designed to prevent the Trump administration from interfering in the state's elections. This is part of an ongoing constitutional standoff between California and the federal government. It signals deepening divisions in US governance heading into the next election cycle — a background political risk for US-focused investors.

stories.title: Gold hits record highs as safe-haven demand rises
stories.why_it_matters: Gold surged to $4,424 an ounce last night — up 0.57% — as investors seek safety amid Middle East tensions and global uncertainty. Gold at these levels reflects genuine fear in markets. For Australian investors, rising gold prices are generally a positive signal for diversified funds with commodity exposure, and they can also support the AUD if Australian gold miners benefit.

markets.summary: The ASX barely moved today, down just 0.01% — essentially flat. Last night in the US, the S&P 500 and NASDAQ both rose modestly. The big story in markets is oil, which cratered 5.7% despite Middle East chaos — a sign traders are more worried about falling demand than supply shortages. Gold hit fresh highs. The AUD is steady around 71.2 US cents.

indicators.name: ASX 200
indicators.note: Essentially flat today — a quiet end to the week for Australian shares.

indicators.name: S&P 500
indicators.note: Modest gain last night — US markets are holding up despite global tensions.

indicators.name: NASDAQ Composite
indicators.note: Tech led the gains last night, up 0.39%. A gentle positive for your US tech holdings.

indicators.name: Crude Oil (WTI)
indicators.note: Big drop — down 5.7% last night despite war escalating in the Middle East. Demand fears are overriding supply worries. Worth watching closely.

indicators.name: Gold
indicators.note: Gold keeps climbing — investors are buying safety as global tensions rise. Near record highs.

indicators.name: AUD/USD
indicators.note: The Aussie dollar is steady, just above 71 US cents. No major moves today.

politics.summary: The main Australian domestic stories this weekend are the RBA's interest rate outlook — with markets now pricing in three more hikes — the government's Digital Duty of Care legislation drawing fierce opposition, and PM Albanese backing stronger AI regulation after meeting Apple's Tim Cook.

stories.title: Traders pricing in three more RBA rate rises — ASX sell-off expected to resume
stories.why_it_matters: Markets are now fully pricing in three more Reserve Bank of Australia rate hikes — meaning the cash rate (currently already elevated) could climb significantly higher still. The AFR reports the ASX is expected to resume selling when trading resumes Monday. Higher rates are bad for growth stocks and property, and put more pressure on mortgage holders. If you've got a variable-rate home loan, this is the story to watch this week.

stories.title: Coalition slams Albanese's 'insidious' Digital Duty of Care laws
stories.why_it_matters: The federal opposition says it is 'absolutely against' Labor's proposed Digital Duty of Care legislation, calling it 'insidious'. The laws would require social media platforms and tech companies to take active steps to protect users (especially kids) from harmful content online — or face big fines. The Coalition's opposition means the bill faces a fight in the Senate. This is shaping up as a major tech-regulation battleground in Australian politics.

stories.title: Albanese backs stronger AI regulation after meeting Apple's Tim Cook
stories.why_it_matters: PM Albanese met with Apple CEO Tim Cook and announced Australia will push for stronger international AI regulation — backing global guardrails on how AI is developed and deployed. This puts Australia at odds with the Trump administration, which is actively opposing AI regulation. For tech investors, the direction of AI regulation in Australia (and globally) matters because it could affect how quickly companies like Google, Microsoft and others can deploy AI products here.

ai.summary: The biggest AI story this weekend is a major antitrust lawsuit against the industry's biggest players — Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and SpaceX AI — alleging they secretly agreed to slow down AI development. Meanwhile, Australia is pushing for stronger AI guardrails.

stories.title: Lawsuit alleges Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and SpaceX AI secretly agreed to slow AI development
stories.why_it_matters: A new antitrust lawsuit (meaning a legal case claiming companies broke competition law) alleges that Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and Elon Musk's SpaceX AI division secretly met and agreed to 'pace' — that is, deliberately slow down — the development of AI. If proven, this would be illegal collusion. The lawsuit is significant because it could reshape how these companies operate and invest in AI, and it directly involves Google, which you hold in your portfolio as GOOG. For now it's early-stage litigation, but it's worth following.

stories.title: Australia pushes big tech to back online safety and AI regulation
stories.why_it_matters: The Australian government is seeking formal backing from big tech companies for its online safety and AI regulation agenda. PM Albanese met with Apple's Tim Cook and others this week as part of this push. Australia wants global tech giants to voluntarily support stronger child safety protections online and clearer rules around AI. The alternative is mandatory legislation — something the tech industry generally prefers to avoid.

stories.title: Albanese backs global AI guardrails as Trump vows to fight regulation
stories.why_it_matters: There's a clear global split opening up on AI regulation: Australia and most Western allies want international guardrails (rules to keep AI safe and accountable), while the Trump administration is actively blocking regulation, arguing it stifles innovation. This tension will shape how AI companies like Google and Microsoft operate in different markets. For long-term tech investors, watch whether the US or the EU/Australia approach wins out — it'll affect profitability and product deployment globally.

sport.summary: It's Finals Week 2 in the NRL, with some big results shaping the preliminary finals. In AFL, Brisbane Lions beat Hawthorn in what's being called a classic finish — but the aftermath has caused controversy.

stories.title: Knights stun Warriors 12-10 to set up Penrith preliminary final
stories.why_it_matters: In a tight game at Eden Park, Auckland, the Newcastle Knights beat the Warriors 12-10 to advance to a preliminary final against Penrith Panthers. The Warriors, playing at home in front of their New Zealand fans, couldn't hold on. The Knights now face the Panthers — the competition's powerhouse — in what shapes as a massive game next week.

stories.title: Roosters demolish Sharks 46-10 in Finals Week 2 opener
stories.why_it_matters: The Sydney Roosters put on a clinic Saturday night at Allianz Stadium, thrashing the Cronulla Sharks 46-10. It was a dominant performance that announces the Roosters as genuine premiership contenders heading into the preliminary finals.

stories.title: Brisbane Lions beat Hawthorn in AFL 'all-time classic' — but controversy follows
stories.why_it_matters: Brisbane Lions beat Hawthorn in what media are calling one of the greatest AFL finals finishes ever. However, the aftermath turned ugly — Lions players were accused of a 'classless' act immediately after the final siren, and the AFL is now investigating after umpires were reportedly targeted in ugly scenes. The AFL has vowed major punishment. The Lions advance to the preliminary final but face scrutiny over their conduct.

stories.title: AFL vows major punishment after umpires targeted in preliminary final
stories.why_it_matters: The AFL has confirmed it will take strong action after umpires were targeted during ugly scenes in the Brisbane-Hawthorn preliminary final. Incidents involving players or supporters abusing match officials are taken extremely seriously by the league. Charges and significant fines or suspensions are expected to be handed down early this week.
